body: Four sentences into talking about his wife of fifty years, a man of seventy-four has to stop and look at the ceiling for a while. It is a Saturday afternoon in a church hall with a hatch through to the kitchen and the urn already on. Somebody has taped a paper banner to the stage and one corner has come away. There are about seventy people and a plate of sandwiches to a table, and everybody waits. Then a woman at the keyboard starts something old, and the room sings it badly, and nobody in that hall would call what is happening a party. It is one.

What that room had was an occasion. Fifty years, a specific man, a specific woman, a thing that actually happened and can be dated. The banner and the urn and the sandwiches were decoration arranged around a fact, and everybody there knew which was which.

There is a version of Christian celebration that has kept the decoration and mislaid the fact. Same build, same drop, same instruction to get your hands in the air, and a chorus that would work equally well about a person, a weekend or a brand.

It is worth taking the word celebrate literally, because it does not mean what the production implies. To celebrate is to mark something — to keep a day, to honour an event, to do publicly what it deserves. The grammar of the word requires an object. You cannot celebrate in general any more than you can remember in general. What has happened in a good deal of modern worship is that the arrangement has been perfected and detached. The lights, the build, the last chorus a semitone up: all of it is technique for producing the feeling that something enormous is being marked, deployed in rooms where nobody has said out loud what.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. Celebration is not treated as a mood to be sprinkled across all of them. It has frequencies of its own, with feast days and calendars behind them.

Naming the occasion costs a song something, which is why it is so often left out. A song about a debt actually settled, by a named person, at a datable moment, cannot be sung by everybody. It will not license for an advert. It narrows the room instead of filling it, and it will always be outsold by a chorus vague enough to project anything onto. The world knows how to throw a party and cannot manufacture the reason for one. We have the reason and keep borrowing the party, because the party is transferable and the reason is not.

The objection here is narrower than the usual killjoy one. Scripture is full of noise. There are trumpets, dancing, a shout that levels a wall, and a king who embarrasses his household in the street. Nobody serious is arguing for restraint as a virtue in itself. The trouble with the borrowed party is not that it is loud but that it is unattached: it produces the physical signature of enormous news without ever stating the news, and a room can run on that for a season and then quietly stop believing there was any.

So celebration on this band sits on frequencies with a calendar behind them rather than being applied as a finish to everything else. Feast days occur when they occur. Songs that name an event air near the event. That arrangement is less flexible than a mood tag and it means a listener meets material out of season, which is the point: a calendar you cannot rearrange is how a family remembers what happened.
None of which means the loud version is cynical. It usually is not.

Be fair to it. A big room with a big sound is hospitable. It gets people through a door who would never have come to a lecture, and there is nothing wrong with a door. Production values are not worldliness, and a person who has had a wretched fortnight can be genuinely lifted by three hundred other people singing something simple at volume. What the borrowed party cannot do is tell you what you came for. It can produce the feeling of an occasion but not the occasion, and the feeling has a short half-life. You leave elated and by Tuesday you could not say what about — which is the signature of a celebration with nothing at the centre.
A song that names nothing can be enjoyed once. It cannot be returned to.

A man in his forties sits at a kitchen table with a laptop open and a mug going cold. He has just made the last payment on something that took eleven years to clear — not a dramatic debt, the ordinary kind, the kind that follows one bad decision at twenty-six and then simply stays. There is no party. His wife is upstairs, the children are at school, and he was going to mention it at dinner. The radio is on over the fridge, and it plays something unmistakably about a debt somebody else settled, in those words, at that length. He sits with his hand over his mouth for about ninety seconds. Then he gets up and takes the mug to the sink, because it is a Thursday and there is a school run at three.

That song did not work because it was loud. It worked because it was about something, and the something was the same shape as what had just happened to him. A song that names its occasion can find the person whose occasion it is. A song that names nothing has nobody to find.

The honest cost of insisting on this is that named celebration is often less immediately enjoyable. A song carrying a specific event has to carry the words of it, and words take room that a hook would otherwise have. Some of it is plainer than you would have chosen, some older, and a certain amount frankly dense — you will meet lyrics that expect you to know a story before the second verse makes sense. As party music, a good deal of it is inferior. That is not a slur but a trade, and it is worth saying out loud.

But the specificity is not a limitation on the joy. It is the supply of it. Delight is proportionate to what is actually the case, which is why the hall full of sandwiches was a better party than most weddings: everybody there knew what they were glad about and could have said it in one sentence. Vagueness is not generosity. It is a way of spending an occasion without naming it. Specificity is also what lets a song survive a second listen, and nothing that cannot survive a second listen has ever done anybody any lasting good.

So the argument is not that the church should be quieter. It is that we are sitting on the one thing the world cannot fake and keep trading it for the one thing the world does better than we do. Anybody can build a room that feels like enormous news. Only one people have the news. Celebration that names what it is celebrating sounds different — usually more specific, often less loud, and it holds up on the twentieth hearing rather than the second.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel and much besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: clean, entertaining, and playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, 40 of them across 29 languages, hosted in their own tongues rather than translated into them afterwards.

If you want to hear the difference, start at HM 304.80 — Celebrate Yeshua! It is the frequency where the occasion is in the name, which is not a marketing decision but a constraint on what can air there. The format is Biblical Music: songs rooted in the text, in the contemporary style people actually listen to, about a specific person and specific things he did. It is neither quiet nor austere. It is simply attached. Play it for an afternoon and notice something odd: after almost any track you can say what was being celebrated, in one sentence, without straining. Then try that with whatever else is on in the car. The difference is not in the production. It is in whether there was an occasion underneath it.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 304.80 on the next time you have an actual occasion — a birthday, a christening, the Friday somebody finally comes home, or the ordinary Thursday when something eleven years long quietly ends at a kitchen table. Do not put it on to raise the temperature of a room; that is the borrowed trick and it works on nobody twice. Put it on because something happened, and let the music be what it is meant to be, which is the decoration arranged around a fact.
